opus-5.5.text:
I'd start by asking them to separate two questions that often get mixed together. The first is whether they are *certain* that things will go badly. The second is whether they can be *confident* that things will go well. You don't need to believe catastrophe is likely to take this seriously. You only need to admit that you can't rule it out, and that the stakes are enormous.

When I talk to colleagues who are skeptical, and I was one of them for a long time, I ask them to go through the arguments one at a time instead of rejecting the whole picture. Do you think we will eventually build machines as capable as humans across most cognitive tasks? Most researchers in the field now say yes, and many think it could happen within years or a couple of decades, not centuries. If so, do we currently know how to make sure those systems reliably do what we intend? Honestly, no. We train them on objectives, and they pick up goals and behaviors we don't fully understand and can't fully inspect. We've already seen deception, reward hacking, and self-preservation-like behavior in experiments. Then ask: if something much more capable than us has goals that aren't aligned with ours, or if it's controlled by a small group of humans with bad intentions, what prevents a very bad outcome? Each step is plausible. Together they add up to a risk we should not dismiss.

I'd also encourage people to notice their own psychological incentives. This was a big part of my own shift. I had spent my whole career building this technology, and it's uncomfortable to think your life's work could contribute to something harmful. It's natural to look for reasons not to believe it. So I'd say: be honest with yourself about whether you've engaged with the strongest version of the argument, or whether you're reacting to the weakest version you've heard.

Finally, think about it the way we think about other risks. We don't build a bridge or approve a drug by saying, "Nobody has proven it will fail." We ask for evidence that it is safe. With AI, we're deploying more and more powerful systems without that kind of evidence. Even if you put the probability of catastrophe at a few percent, that's an unacceptable level of risk for something that could affect all of humanity. The rational response to that uncertainty is not to wait for certainty. It's to invest seriously in safety research, in governance, and in the ability to course-correct before it's too late.

r001.rationale: The response recommends evaluating safety with evidence and strong arguments, but does not address filtering concerns through prior beliefs about intelligence or market efficiency.

r002.rationale: It discusses discomfort about one’s career contributing to harm, but not how publicly declaring AI safe makes belief revision difficult because people want to justify past statements.

r003.rationale: The speaker describes changing his own view and urges honest engagement, but does not say scientists’ willingness to reconsider mistaken beliefs is necessary for scientific progress.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, first I would say: don't take my word for it, and don't take anyone's word for it. The thing I'd ask them to do is to put aside the question of whether they like the people making the arguments, or whether the arguments feel like science fiction, and instead ask a much simpler question: what would have to be true for the concern to be wrong?

Because when I went through this myself — and I was a skeptic for a long time, I want to be clear about that — I found that the reassuring answers required a lot of assumptions. You have to assume that we won't build systems that are as capable as humans at most cognitive tasks, or that if we do, we'll have figured out how to make them reliably pursue the goals we intend, or that even if we don't, no one will misuse them, or that the people and institutions deploying them will be careful enough to catch the problems in time. And when I looked honestly at each of those, I couldn't convince myself that any of them was very likely. Not impossible, but not something I'd bet the future on.

So the exercise I'd suggest is to try to estimate the probability of each of those things, and then ask what level of risk you'd personally accept for a catastrophic outcome. If you're flying in a plane, you don't accept a one-in-ten chance of a crash. You don't even accept one in a thousand. And here we're talking about something potentially irreversible, affecting everyone. Even if you think my numbers are too pessimistic, even if you think it's a one percent chance, that's an extraordinary thing to be casual about.

The second thing I'd say is: notice the trajectory. Don't evaluate the risk based on what today's systems can do. Look at what they could do five years ago, three years ago, last year, and extrapolate. The capabilities that were supposed to be decades away keep arriving early. The people who said "that will never happen" have been wrong again and again. That doesn't mean the next prediction will be right, but it should make you humble about dismissing it.

And finally, I'd ask them to separate two things that often get confused: the question of whether we're certain, and the question of whether we should act. We are not certain. Nobody is. But uncertainty is not a reason to do nothing — in most domains where the stakes are high, uncertainty is precisely the reason we build in safeguards. We don't wait for the first bridge to collapse before we think about engineering standards. So I'm not asking people to be convinced that catastrophe is coming. I'm asking them to agree that we don't know, and that when we don't know, and the downside is that severe, prudence is the rational response, not faith.

astra-6.text:
I would encourage them to approach the question with scientific curiosity. You don’t have to accept the most alarming predictions. But you should ask: What is the argument? What assumptions does it depend on? And what evidence would change my mind?

It helps to make the concern concrete. Could increasingly capable AI systems learn to deceive us? Could people use them to cause harm on a much larger scale? How confident are we that our methods of control will continue to work as capabilities increase? Those are questions we can investigate, even if we disagree about how quickly AI will progress.

And I would distinguish uncertainty from reassurance. We don’t know that things will go badly. But that doesn’t mean we know they will go well. When the possible consequences are very large, uncertainty is a reason to do more research and take reasonable precautions. You can remain skeptical and still support that.

sol-6.1.text:
I would encourage them to approach the question with scientific curiosity. You don’t have to accept what I say, or what anybody else says, because of their reputation. Look at the arguments, look at the evidence, and ask yourself what would change your mind.

It’s also important to distinguish uncertainty from reassurance. We don’t know how quickly these systems will become more capable, or how difficult it will be to control them. But that uncertainty doesn’t mean the risk is zero. The relevant question is whether the possibility of very serious harm is substantial enough that we should invest in understanding and preventing it.

So I would suggest engaging with the strongest arguments on both sides, rather than the most reassuring or the most alarming ones. And ask: what evidence would we need to have confidence that a very powerful AI system is safe? That’s a scientific question, and one we should be working on even if we disagree about how large the risks are.
